tagline: Eleven miles of bay views, clay bluffs and a surviving mill chimney
intro: Pensacola Scenic Bluffs Highway follows 11 miles of U.S. 90 beside Escambia Bay, with two-lane roadway, residential stretches, parks and open space. Designated a Florida Scenic Highway on April 24, 1998, it offers views from bluffs that FDOT identifies as the highest points along Florida’s coastline. Wetlands occupy its northern end, while clay deposits recall the shoreline’s brickmaking history.

The road’s role changed abruptly after Hurricane Ivan damaged the I-10 bay bridge in 2004. Interstate traffic moved onto U.S. 90 while temporary spans were built, and motorists waited as long as two hours at the Escambia River crossing. A replacement I-10 bridge followed, and Scenic Highway’s overpass at the interchange was replaced in 2015. The new interstate bridge took an alignment south of the original crossing, which stayed in place during construction, and expanded the crossing from four lanes to six.

Traveling south begins in the Escambia River wetlands and follows the shore past Macky Bay and the I-10 interchange in Ferry Pass. Chimney Park marks Red Bluff at Langley Avenue; farther toward Pensacola, the road follows the bay past residential neighborhoods and parkland. At Perry Avenue, Scenic Highway gives way to Cervantes Street.

moments.title: Escambia River
moments.text: U.S. 90 crosses the Escambia River amid tidal wetlands at the northern end of the scenic drive. The crossing became a bottleneck after Hurricane Ivan struck in September 2004. Storm surge knocked 58 spans off the I-10 bay bridges and misaligned another 66. Traffic shifted to U.S. 90, where drivers waited as long as two hours to cross between Escambia and Santa Rosa counties. The river feeds Escambia Bay, which connects to open water through Pensacola Bay.

moments.title: Chimney Park
moments.text: A single chimney marks the Hyer-Knowles mill at Red Bluff. The steam-powered sawmill dated to 1854. When Confederate forces abandoned Pensacola in 1862, mills were destroyed to keep them from Union use. Braxton Bragg ordered the destruction of this mill. The chimney survived and now belongs to Chimney Park, a wayside park along U.S. 90 opposite Langley Avenue. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in May 2012.
moments.notice: The mill’s chimney is the only surviving part of its building.

moments.title: Bay Bluffs Park
moments.text: Bay Bluffs Park overlooks Escambia Bay. Its view belongs to a shoreline of high bluffs and clay deposits once used to make bricks. The bay connects to open water through Pensacola Bay to the southeast.
moments.notice: Escambia Bay lies below Bay Bluffs Park.

sources.label: Florida Department of Transportation, Pensacola Scenic Bluffs Highway
